rv.q: This is a communal celebration, reaching a climax in a round of quietly affecting bell-ringing.
Terera is a sensational Scrooge, swinging from uncompromising severity in the early scenes to joy of such giddiness that it makes you want to dance in the aisles.
From the mince pies and satsumas given out as you enter, to the impossibly jaunty cast and falling snow, this is a Christmas production that still warms you to your core.
A CHRISTMAS CAROL is charm itself, runs 2 hours and 20 mins (including interval), and continues until 9th January 2027.

Jack Thorne's script is pitched so an eight-year-old can follow it, then slips in things the parents will recognise, and the children only will later: deep regret, the lifelong impact of bad parenting, love postponed until it has gone, and how quickly a life folds itself away.

A Christmas Carol is nicely conceived as an interactive experience – right down to the Old Vic’s air con, which proves as icy as Scrooge’s heart – but 10 years on, the adaptation itself is rather thin.
This production is missing hues and shadows of previous ones.
Thorne and Warchus do a beautiful job of bringing a crotchety London crowd together, with much Christmas cheer for adults and children alike, and a hot mince pie to boot.
Even if you are sick to death of the story or struggle to find the Christmas spirit yourself, this joyous and beautiful production could melt the heart of even the toughest of cynics.

The Old Vic's A Christmas Carol remains a lovely festive treat that can warm even the coldest of hearts.
The production wholeheartedly embraces the spirit of the season, bringing the festivities to life in rather spectacular fashion.

World-class staging defines this production, with Rob Howell's simple designs being ingeniously lit by Hugh Vanstone.

The production value is the main highlight.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this 10th-anniversary Old Vic production as a beloved festive institution, with Giles Terera's Scrooge earning particular acclaim. A handful find it more spectacle than substance, but most agree it remains essential Christmas theatre.
